patient.name: Ciaran Doherty
patient.complaint: Tired all the time, aching knuckles and knees, and reduced libido for a year
background: Irish family; his uncle had 'liver trouble'
Drinks 14 units of alcohol a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' in a middle-aged man of Northern European ancestry with fatigue, arthropathy, diabetes, low libido, skin 'tanning' and abnormal LFTs, with Wilson's, alpha-1 antitrypsin and autoimmune hepatitis as distractors.

points: Aching **knuckles and knees**; erections and libido reduced.
Diabetes diagnosed 6 months ago, not overweight.
His wife says he looks **tanned** all year round.

steps.lead: Ciaran's symptoms span **liver, pancreas, joints, gonads and skin**: the organs where excess iron is deposited.
A **man** of **Northern European (Irish)** descent with an affected relative: classic for **autosomal recessive HFE** disease.

points: Bronze-grey skin, most obvious on his face and hands.
Liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.
Swollen, tender **2nd and 3rd MCP joints**; small testes.

visual.title: Where to feel
visual.caption: **Hepatomegaly** in the RUQ: the liver is the main iron store and the first organ damaged.

steps.lead: Every finding fits: fatigue, **diabetes**, arthropathy, **bronze skin**, hepatomegaly and **testicular atrophy**.
Ciaran has two of the triad, **diabetes and bronze skin**; whether he has the third, **cirrhosis**, decides his prognosis.

steps.q: Which diagnosis best explains Ciaran's diabetes, arthropathy, low libido and tanned skin?
steps.r: **Haemochromatosis** links all of them via iron deposition. Wilson's presents younger, with neuropsychiatric signs.

steps.title: Haemochromatosis vs look-alikes
head: Feature
Haemochromatosis
Wilson's disease
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
rows: Diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy, low libido

steps.lead: Ciaran already has the **commonest endocrine complication (diabetes)** and probably the **second (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism)**; cirrhosis brings **HCC** risk.

steps.text: Women present **later** because menstruation and pregnancy shed iron; suspect it in a post-menopausal woman with the same picture.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (transferrin saturation) or 'diagnostic investigation' (HFE genotyping), and iron study patterns: a raised ferritin alone does not confirm it.

steps.q: Which test should be done first for Ciaran?
steps.r: **Transferrin saturation** is the initial test. Ferritin alone is non-specific (inflammation, alcohol, NAFLD).

steps.title: Ciaran's bloods
steps.text: High saturation **and** high ferritin; low testosterone with **low LH**: a pituitary (hypogonadotrophic) cause.

visual.title: Transferrin saturation
visual.label: Ciaran 82%
visual.caption: A raised transferrin saturation is the **first** abnormal result in haemochromatosis.

steps.lead: Ciaran's **transferrin saturation** came first and was high; his **ferritin** was then checked and is also high.

steps.text: A high ferritin with a **normal** transferrin saturation is usually alcohol, NAFLD or inflammation, not haemochromatosis.

points: His sister and children are offered testing.

steps.lead: Ciaran's **iron studies** plus **homozygous C282Y** on HFE testing confirm hereditary haemochromatosis.

steps.text: Ferritin above about **1000 µg/L** or raised ALT raises the chance of cirrhosis; this is when specialists assess liver fibrosis.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (venesection), when desferrioxamine replaces it (anaemia, sickle cell disease), and lifestyle advice (no iron or vitamin C supplements, care with raw shellfish, reduce alcohol).

steps.q: What is first-line treatment for Ciaran?
steps.r: **Venesection** removes iron directly. Penicillamine is for **Wilson's**; desferrioxamine is second-line.

steps.lead: Ciaran starts **weekly venesection** with ferritin and transferrin saturation monitored.

visual.title: Ciaran's ferritin on venesection
visual.caption: Weekly venesection until ferritin is low (about **50 µg/L**), then maintenance every few months.

steps.lead: Ciaran is not anaemic, so venesection suits him. **Desferrioxamine** is for those who cannot be venesected, such as **anaemia** or **sickle cell disease**.
Ciaran is told: no iron tablets, no **vitamin C** supplements or big glasses of orange juice, cut alcohol, avoid **raw shellfish**.

steps.title: Ciaran's plan
nodes: Weekly venesection; monitor ferritin and TSAT
Diet: no iron or vitamin C supplements
Treat complications: diabetes, liver, heart, testosterone

steps.lead: If Ciaran developed an **arrhythmia**, decompensated cirrhosis or a liver mass, that would need **urgent** specialist management.
Ciaran's family is screened through the **HFE genetic testing pathway**.

steps.text: Venesection does **not** reverse cirrhosis or established arthropathy. Ciaran's cardiomyopathy and fatigue may improve; joint pain often does not.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on the mode of inheritance (autosomal recessive), the HFE C282Y mutation, the hepcidin-ferroportin mechanism, and why iron in the pituitary gives hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism.

steps.lead: Ciaran's **C282Y** mutation makes his liver produce too little **hepcidin**, so his gut keeps absorbing iron despite overload.

steps.title: From HFE mutation to organ damage
nodes: High iron absorption from the duodenum
Iron deposits in liver, pancreas, heart, pituitary, joints, skin

steps.q: Ciaran and his wife (not a carrier) ask about their children. What is the chance each child is affected?
steps.r: **Autosomal recessive**: with a non-carrier partner, every child gets one faulty copy and is a **carrier**, not affected.

steps.lead: Iron in Ciaran's **pancreas** caused his diabetes; in his **pituitary**, low LH and testosterone; in his **skin**, more melanin.

steps.text: Low LH/FSH with low testosterone means a **pituitary** cause (hypogonadotrophic). Primary testicular damage would give **high** LH/FSH.

mcq.q: What is the classic triad of haemochromatosis?
What is the most common endocrine complication of haemochromatosis?
Which malignancy is a risk in haemochromatosis with cirrhosis?
What is the initial investigation for suspected haemochromatosis?
Which mutation is classically found on HFE testing?
mcq.r: **C282Y**. ATP7B is Wilson's; F508del is CF.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for haemochromatosis?
When is desferrioxamine used instead of venesection?
o: When there is anaemia or sickle cell disease
mcq.r: When venesection is **unsuitable**: anaemia or sickle cell disease.

mcq.q: Which dietary advice is given in haemochromatosis?
mcq.r: **Vitamin C increases iron absorption**; also avoid iron supplements and raw shellfish.

mcq.q: What is the mode of inheritance of hereditary haemochromatosis?
Which hormone is inappropriately low in HFE haemochromatosis?
mcq.r: Low **hepcidin** fails to suppress ferroportin, so absorption stays high.

technique.stem: A 48 year old man has a 12 month history of tiredness, pain in his knuckles and reduced libido. He was diagnosed with diabetes last year despite a BMI of 23 kg/m². His skin looks tanned although he has not been abroad. His liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis: find the one condition that explains every system involved.

clues: diagnosed with diabetes last year despite a BMI of 23
steps.x: Arthropathy, hypogonadism, diabetes, bronze skin, hepatomegaly, **very high ferritin**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemochromatosis**: iron in joints, pituitary, pancreas, skin and liver.

elim: Addison's pigments skin but causes hypotension and weight loss, not diabetes or hepatomegaly.
A1AT gives emphysema and liver disease, not diabetes or pigmentation.
Autoimmune hepatitis affects young women; no diabetes or pigmentation.
Wilson's presents younger with neuropsychiatric signs.

steps.x: **D. Haemochromatosis.** Rule: diabetes + bronze skin + liver + joints + low libido = iron overload.

technique.stem: A 55 year old man has a raised ferritin of 640 µg/L on routine bloods. He drinks 40 units of alcohol a week and has a BMI of 31 kg/m². He has no symptoms. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: The next test after a raised ferritin.
Alcohol and obesity (NAFLD) both raise ferritin; ferritin alone does not confirm iron overload.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Check **transferrin saturation**: if normal, iron overload is unlikely.

elim: HFE testing follows a raised transferrin saturation.
Biopsy is not an early test.
MRI is for specialist quantification later.
Caeruloplasmin is for Wilson's disease.

steps.x: **E. Transferrin saturation.** Rule: raised ferritin alone does not confirm it; TSAT is the initial test.

technique.stem: A 46 year old man has newly diagnosed hereditary haemochromatosis and is starting venesection. He asks about his diet. He takes an over-the-counter multivitamin with iron and drinks a litre of orange juice daily. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Eat more red meat and liver
Stop the iron multivitamin and reduce orange juice

steps.x: Lifestyle advice in haemochromatosis.

clues: a litre of orange juice daily
steps.x: Extra iron plus **vitamin C**, which increases iron absorption.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop iron supplements; avoid excess vitamin C.

elim: Vitamin C increases iron absorption.
His current diet adds iron and vitamin C.
That adds dietary iron.
A strict iron-free diet is impractical and unnecessary; venesection does the work.

steps.x: **E. Stop the iron multivitamin and reduce orange juice.** Rule: no iron, no excess vitamin C, care with raw shellfish.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman's brother has hereditary haemochromatosis and is homozygous for C282Y. Her parents are both well. She has genetic testing and is found to be heterozygous for C282Y. Her partner has no HFE mutation.
technique.q: Which is the probability that each of her children will be homozygous for C282Y?

steps.x: An inheritance calculation.
Autosomal recessive: parents are carriers; she is a carrier; partner is not.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Carrier × non-carrier: children are 50% carriers, **0% homozygous**.

elim: 25% needs both parents to be carriers.
50% is the chance of being a carrier, not affected.
Not possible with recessive inheritance from one carrier.
Needs both parents homozygous.

steps.x: **A. 0%.** Rule: autosomal recessive; you need two faulty copies to be affected.

practice.stem: A 56 year old man of Scottish descent has increasing tiredness and abdominal discomfort. He has diabetes and erectile dysfunction. He has bronze-grey skin pigmentation, palmar erythema, spider naevi and a firm liver edge. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Cirrhosis, diabetes and bronze skin is the classic haemochromatosis triad, confirmed by very high transferrin saturation and ferritin. Alcohol can raise ferritin but not transferrin saturation to this degree, and no alcohol history is given.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a man with chronic liver disease: what links the extras?
Triad of **cirrhosis, diabetes, bronze skin**; TSAT 88%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemochromatosis** with cirrhosis.

elim: No alcohol history; does not explain bronze skin or TSAT 88%.
A1AT gives emphysema, not diabetes or pigmentation.
PBC is cholestatic in middle-aged women with itch.
Wilson's presents younger with neurological signs.

steps.x: **C. Haemochromatosis.** Rule: cirrhosis + diabetes + bronze skin = haemochromatosis.

practice.stem: A 54 year old man with hereditary haemochromatosis has had painful, swollen knees for 6 months. He also has stiffness in his 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. An X-ray of his knees is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the knee X-ray?
practice.e: Haemochromatosis arthropathy is associated with calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout), which shows as chondrocalcinosis, linear calcification of the cartilage.

steps.x: An X-ray finding in haemochromatosis arthropathy.
Large-joint arthropathy plus MCP involvement: the iron arthropathy pattern.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chondrocalcinosis** (pseudogout).

elim: Pencil-in-cup is psoriatic arthritis.
Periarticular erosions and osteopenia are rheumatoid arthritis.
Punched-out erosions are gout.
Sacroiliitis is ankylosing spondylitis; not a knee finding.

steps.x: **A. Chondrocalcinosis.** Rule: haemochromatosis arthropathy = pseudogout/chondrocalcinosis.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man with hereditary haemochromatosis has a 9 month history of low libido and erectile dysfunction. He shaves less often. His testes are small. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Low testosterone with low LH and FSH means a pituitary cause: iron deposition in the pituitary gives hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, the second most common endocrine complication of haemochromatosis.

steps.x: The cause of hypogonadism: read the LH and FSH.
Low testosterone **and low LH/FSH**; normal prolactin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism** from pituitary iron.

elim: Steroid misuse suppresses LH, but there is no history and it would not fit his iron disease.
Primary failure gives **high** LH/FSH.
Prolactin is normal.
Low testosterone is an organic cause.

steps.x: **B. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism.** Rule: low testosterone + low LH = pituitary; in haemochromatosis, think iron.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with haemochromatosis and cirrhosis has lost 6 kg in 3 months and has right upper quadrant discomfort. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a 4 cm solid lesion in the right lobe of the liver.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Cirrhosis from haemochromatosis carries a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; weight loss, a solid liver lesion and a very high AFP confirm it.

steps.x: A liver mass in a cirrhotic: think about the complications of cirrhosis.
Cirrhosis + weight loss + solid mass + **AFP 860**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hepatocellular carcinoma**.

elim: Cholangiocarcinoma gives obstructive jaundice; AFP is not raised.
FNH is benign in young women; AFP normal.
Adenoma is linked to the oral contraceptive pill.
Abscess gives fever and a cystic lesion.

steps.x: **D. Hepatocellular carcinoma.** Rule: haemochromatosis + cirrhosis = HCC risk.

practice.stem: A 44 year old man has 3 months of breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. He has diabetes and slate-grey skin pigmentation. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 108/70 mmHg. JVP is raised and there is hepatomegaly. Coronary angiography is normal. Echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 32%.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his heart failure?
practice.e: Cardiomyopathy with AF in a young man with diabetes, pigmentation, hepatomegaly and grossly raised iron studies is iron-overload cardiomyopathy from haemochromatosis. Normal coronaries exclude ischaemia. It can improve with venesection.

steps.x: The cause of a cardiomyopathy: what systemic disease fits?
Diabetes + pigmentation + cardiomyopathy + AF; iron studies very high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemochromatosis** cardiomyopathy.

elim: No alcohol history.
Amyloid gives a thick, restrictive heart, not pigmentation and diabetes.
Sarcoid causes heart block and lung disease.
Coronaries are normal.

steps.x: **D. Haemochromatosis.** Rule: diabetes + bronze skin + cardiomyopathy = iron; it improves with venesection.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman, 6 years after the menopause, has fatigue and joint pains in her hands. Her BMI is 24 kg/m² and she drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. Her father had diabetes and cirrhosis. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A raised transferrin saturation with high ferritin, arthropathy and a suggestive family history in a post-menopausal woman is hereditary haemochromatosis. Women present later because menstruation removes iron.

steps.x: Diagnosis: is the ferritin from iron overload or something else?

clues: Her father had diabetes and cirrhosis
steps.x: TSAT 71% (true overload), normal CRP, little alcohol, normal BMI, family history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hereditary haemochromatosis** presenting after the menopause.

elim: 4 units a week is too little.
BMI is normal and NAFLD does not raise TSAT this much.
CRP is normal and RA does not raise TSAT.
Still's gives fever, rash and very high ferritin with high CRP.

steps.x: **B. Hereditary haemochromatosis.** Rule: high TSAT + high ferritin = iron overload; women present after menopause.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man of Irish descent has fatigue, arthralgia and newly diagnosed diabetes. His GP suspects hereditary haemochromatosis and requests iron studies. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely pattern of results?
practice.e: In haemochromatosis transferrin saturation is raised first, then ferritin rises as iron accumulates. Low ferritin with low saturation is iron deficiency.

steps.x: The iron study pattern in iron overload.

clues: fatigue, arthralgia and newly diagnosed diabetes
steps.x: Established, symptomatic disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **High TSAT and high ferritin**.

elim: High ferritin with low TSAT suggests inflammation or anaemia of chronic disease.
Ferritin is raised once overload is established.
That is iron deficiency.
Not iron overload.

steps.x: **A. High ferritin, high transferrin saturation.** Rule: TSAT rises first, ferritin follows.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has fatigue and arthralgia. His iron studies are abnormal on two occasions. He has no history of blood transfusion or alcohol excess. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Raised transferrin saturation and ferritin are followed by HFE genetic testing for C282Y, which confirms hereditary haemochromatosis. Liver biopsy is now rarely needed.

steps.x: **Diagnostic** test after abnormal iron studies.

clues: iron studies are abnormal on two occasions
no history of blood transfusion or alcohol excess
steps.x: TSAT 76% and ferritin 1120; no secondary cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HFE genotyping** (C282Y).

elim: Bone marrow iron is not used to diagnose haemochromatosis.
Biopsy is reserved for assessing fibrosis, not diagnosis.
Delaying adds nothing; results are already repeated.
Caeruloplasmin is for Wilson's.

steps.x: **B. HFE genotyping.** Rule: high TSAT + high ferritin → HFE C282Y test.

practice.stem: A 51 year old man is diagnosed with hereditary haemochromatosis. He is homozygous for C282Y. He has fatigue but no cirrhosis on assessment. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Venesection is first-line: it removes iron directly, monitored with ferritin and transferrin saturation. He has a normal haemoglobin, so there is no reason to use chelation.

steps.x: First-line treatment for confirmed haemochromatosis.
Normal haemoglobin, so he can be venesected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Venesection**.

elim: Desferrioxamine is second-line when venesection is unsuitable.
Diet alone cannot remove stored iron.
Chelation is not first-line in HFE disease.
Penicillamine is for Wilson's disease.

steps.x: **E. Venesection.** Rule: haemochromatosis = venesection first; chelation only if anaemic.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man with sickle cell disease has had many blood transfusions. He has iron overload with liver and cardiac involvement. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his iron overload?
practice.e: Venesection is unsuitable when the patient is anaemic, such as in sickle cell disease, so an iron chelator such as desferrioxamine is used.

steps.x: How to remove iron in someone who cannot lose blood.
Anaemic (Hb 78) with severe overload.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Desferrioxamine** chelation.

elim: B12 does not treat iron overload.
That worsens overload.
Penicillamine chelates copper (Wilson's).
Venesection would worsen his anaemia.

steps.x: **A. Desferrioxamine.** Rule: iron overload + anaemia or sickle cell = chelation, not venesection.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with hereditary haemochromatosis has compensated cirrhosis. After a year of venesection his ferritin is 48 µg/L and he is on maintenance venesection. He feels well. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Venesection does not reverse cirrhosis, so he remains at risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and needs 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance (NICE). Transplant is for decompensation or HCC.

steps.x: Long-term follow-up once iron is controlled.
Iron controlled, but **cirrhosis persists**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HCC surveillance**: 6-monthly ultrasound.

elim: CT chest is not HCC surveillance.
Cirrhosis still needs follow-up.
He is compensated, so transplant is not indicated now.
Iron will reaccumulate without maintenance.

steps.x: **D. Liver ultrasound every 6 months.** Rule: cirrhosis from haemochromatosis = lifelong HCC surveillance.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man is homozygous for the HFE C282Y mutation. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. His transferrin saturation is 79% and ferritin 1300 µg/L. Despite this iron overload, his duodenum continues to absorb dietary iron at a high rate.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his continued iron absorption?
o: Low hepcidin failing to suppress ferroportin
Mutation in ferroportin making it hyperactive
Reduced iron loss in the stool
practice.e: HFE C282Y causes inappropriately low hepcidin. Hepcidin normally degrades ferroportin; without it, ferroportin keeps exporting iron from enterocytes into the blood despite overload.

steps.x: Why absorption stays high in HFE disease.

clues: homozygous for the HFE C282Y mutation
steps.x: The body's iron brake has failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low hepcidin** → ferroportin unchecked.

elim: EPO drives iron use in anaemia; he is not anaemic.
Transferrin carries iron; it does not drive absorption.
Ferroportin itself is normal in HFE disease.
Stool loss is not the mechanism.

steps.x: **C. Low hepcidin failing to suppress ferroportin.** Rule: HFE → low hepcidin → high absorption.

prompts.q: What is haemochromatosis, who gets it, and how is it inherited?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you the ancestry and the sex.

points.why: Liver, pancreas, heart, joints, pituitary/gonads, skin.
Irish or Scottish names in the stem are a clue.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and examination findings of haemochromatosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: count how many systems are involved.

points.p: Erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, testicular atrophy
Hepatomegaly and signs of chronic liver disease
points.why: Liver is the main iron store.

prompts.q: What is the classic triad and what are the complications?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: rank the endocrine complications.

points.p: Diabetes is the most common endocrine complication; hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism second

prompts.q: How do you tell haemochromatosis apart from Wilson's disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these are the standard distractors for metabolic liver disease.

points.p: Haemochromatosis: iron, middle age, diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy
Wilson's: copper, young, neuropsychiatric, Kayser-Fleischer rings
Alpha-1 antitrypsin: emphysema plus liver disease

prompts.q: What is the first test, the second test and the confirmatory test?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: initial vs diagnostic investigation are both asked.

points.p: Raised ferritin alone does not confirm it
points.why: Alcohol, NAFLD and inflammation raise it.

prompts.q: What is the first-line treatment, and when is second-line used?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check the haemoglobin before choosing.

points.p: When venesection unsuitable: anaemia or sickle cell disease

prompts.q: What long-term advice and complication management does a patient need?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the advice options include traps about vitamin C and shellfish.

points.p: Avoid excess vitamin C (e.g. orange juice)
Manage diabetes, liver, heart and endocrine complications; urgent care for arrhythmia, decompensation or HCC

prompts.q: What is the molecular mechanism of HFE haemochromatosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hepcidin and ferroportin are the two words to know.

points.p: Ferroportin not suppressed, so absorption stays high
points.why: Iron exported from enterocytes despite overload.

points.p: Organ damage via oxidative stress and fibrosis

prompts.q: Why does haemochromatosis cause diabetes, hypogonadism, cardiomyopathy and bronze skin?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: map each organ to its consequence.

points.p: Pancreatic iron impairs insulin secretion: bronze diabetes
Skin: increased melanin plus dermal iron

glossary.Haemochromatosis: Inherited disorder of excess iron absorption, causing iron deposition in organs.
glossary.HFE: Gene regulating hepcidin; mutations cause hereditary haemochromatosis.
glossary.C282Y: The classic HFE mutation; homozygosity causes most hereditary haemochromatosis.
glossary.Autosomal recessive: Inheritance needing two faulty copies to be affected; carriers are usually well.
glossary.Hepcidin: Liver hormone that reduces iron absorption by degrading ferroportin.
glossary.Ferroportin: Iron exporter on gut and macrophage cells that releases iron into the blood.
glossary.Transferrin saturation: Percentage of transferrin carrying iron; the first test, raised in haemochromatosis.
glossary.Ferritin: Iron storage protein; high in iron overload but also in inflammation, alcohol and NAFLD.
glossary.Iron overload: Too much total body iron, deposited in organs and causing damage.
glossary.Bronze diabetes: Diabetes plus bronze skin from iron in the pancreas and skin.
glossary.Hyperpigmentation: Darkening of the skin; bronze or slate-grey in haemochromatosis.
glossary.Arthropathy: Joint disease; in haemochromatosis, typically 2nd/3rd MCPs and large joints.
glossary.Chondrocalcinosis: Calcium deposits in joint cartilage seen on X-ray, linked to pseudogout.
glossary.Pseudogout: Joint inflammation from calcium pyrophosphate crystals; associated with haemochromatosis.
glossary.Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism: Low sex hormones because the pituitary makes too little LH and FSH.
glossary.LH: Luteinising hormone; pituitary hormone driving testosterone production.
glossary.FSH: Follicle-stimulating hormone; pituitary hormone controlling sperm and egg development.
glossary.Testicular atrophy: Shrunken testes; a sign of hypogonadism.
glossary.Cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with nodules; irreversible.
glossary.Hepatomegaly: Enlarged liver, felt below the right costal margin.
glossary.HCC: Hepatocellular carcinoma: primary liver cancer, a risk in cirrhosis.
glossary.Alpha-fetoprotein: Blood tumour marker raised in hepatocellular carcinoma.
glossary.Cardiomyopathy: Heart muscle disease; iron causes restrictive or dilated forms.
glossary.Venesection: Therapeutic removal of blood (usually 450 to 500 mL) to remove iron.
glossary.Phlebotomy: Drawing blood from a vein; therapeutic phlebotomy is venesection.
glossary.Desferrioxamine: Injected iron chelator used when venesection is unsuitable.
glossary.Chelation: Using a drug that binds a metal so it can be excreted.
glossary.Sickle cell disease: Inherited haemoglobin disorder; transfusions cause iron overload and venesection is unsuitable.
glossary.Wilson's disease: Autosomal recessive copper overload with liver and neuropsychiatric disease.
glossary.Kayser-Fleischer rings: Copper-brown rings at the edge of the cornea in Wilson's disease.
glossary.Caeruloplasmin: Copper-carrying protein; low in Wilson's disease.
glossary.Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: Inherited lack of a protease inhibitor causing emphysema and liver disease.
glossary.Oxidative stress: Cell damage from reactive oxygen species, which free iron helps generate.
glossary.Cascade screening: Testing relatives of someone with an inherited condition.
glossary.Penicillamine: Copper chelator used in Wilson's disease, not haemochromatosis.
